problem_statement: The paper frames the problem as generating samples and time series from stochastic differential equations, especially when one wants samples at times different from the initial point for financial analysis and dataset augmentation. It also treats learning a quantile function from data and propagating it in time as the core task.
problem_statement_quotes: We propose a quantum algorithm for sampling from a solution of stochastic diﬀerential equations (SDEs).

The task then falls into the category of data-driven machine learning problems, which has attracted attention recently [14, 15]. Also, a (potentially implicit) solution of the FP equation does not oﬀer strategies to generate samples directly.
classical_baseline: The paper compares against classical inversion sampling, Euler-Maruyama simulation of SDEs, and classical generative modelling approaches such as GANs. It also mentions classical quantile-function learning as a possible neural representation of the target distribution.
classical_baseline_quotes: Second, Eq. (1) can be integrated using the Euler-Maruyama method [16], where the deterministic part of the diﬀerential equation is solved with stepwise propagation, and the Wiener process is modelled with a random number generator.
This corresponds to the ensemble generation process (broadly speaking, generative modelling), which is computationally challenging for complex models.
Motivated by classical GAN successes [22, 53], various protocols for the adversarial training of generative quantum models were proposed, and coined as qGANs [54, 55].
In this work, we suggest to shift the focus to the very tool that enables sampling — the quantile function (QF) (not to be mistaken with the quantile of a distribution).
classical_difficulty: The paper says the classical route is hard because inverting the CDF is often a transcendental problem without a closed-form solution, and because direct sampling from complicated multidimensional distributions at different times is computationally expensive. It also says Euler-Maruyama-based ensemble generation is challenging for complex models and hindered by the curse of dimensionality.
classical_difficulty_quotes: In most cases this leads to a transcendental problem without a closed-form solution. This poses computational challenges and requires graphical solution methods [80].
Namely, drawing x ∼p(x, t) from a com- plicated multidimensional distribution, at diﬀerent t, represents another computationally expensive problem to solve.
For multidimen- sional systems this is hindered by the curse of dimensionality.
The task of solving random partial diﬀerential equations was recently addressed with deep learning using physics-informed neural networks [17–19].
business_stakes: The paper explicitly ties the motivation to financial analysis, dataset augmentation, financial calculus, and pricing financial derivatives. It also mentions interest rates, bond prices, currency exchange rates, and Forex pair trading as application contexts.
business_stakes_quotes: SDEs are widely used in ﬁnancial calculus [11], a fundamental component of all mechanisms of pricing ﬁnancial derivatives and descrip- tion of market dynamics.
Potential applications of SDEs in ﬁnance lie in predicting stock prices, currency exchange rates and more [12].
In ﬁnancial analysis its generalization is known as the Vasicek model [89]. It describes the evolution of interest rates and bond prices [90].
We also note that OU describes dynamics of currency exchange rates, and is commonly used in Forex pair trading — a primary example for quantum generative modelling explored to date [70, 71].
extraction_notes: Motivation is explicit and spread across abstract and introduction; paper is primarily about SDE-based generative modelling with finance examples.
